video_title: Some AI Lessons In A Booming Economy
gist: Ed Yardeni argues the AI trade is deflating rather than bursting, with S&P 500 forward earnings up 49% since Liberation Day while the forward P/E fell to 18.2, so this is not 1999-2000. He keeps a 7,900 year-end and 10,000-by-2029 target (possibly reached by end-2027), expects more Fed hikes from 3%-handle inflation, and calls gold's drop a correction.

insights.claim: Yardeni welcomes air coming out of the AI bubble, arguing that a gradual deflation means the AI bubble will not burst or cause a systemic calamity for the economy or stock market.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: AI selloffs are a healthy de-risking, not a precursor to crash.
insights.quote: I don't really have a problem here with some air coming out of the AI bubble. Um if that's what's happening then the AI bubble is not going to burst.

insights.claim: Friday's sharp selloff in AI-related stocks saw money rotate into consumer staples and healthcare; only 2 of 11 S&P 500 sectors (information technology and healthcare) were down for the week, which Yardeni frames as welcome market broadening.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Rotation out of AI into defensives broadens the market rather than sinking it.

insights.claim: If the bond market makes borrowing more expensive for 'dodgier' AI plays, it is effectively regulating the AI arms race and allocating capital appropriately, which Yardeni views as a good thing.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Credit spreads widening on weak AI borrowers is a feature, not a systemic threat.
insights.quote: if the bond market is going to regulate uh the the AI trade uh by making it more expensive to borrow for some of the dodgier AI plays, uh that's a good thing.

insights.claim: Neoclouds resemble dotcoms in lacking visible earnings and may burn cash and go bust, but unlike dotcoms (left with PCs and desks) they own GPUs and data centers and would likely be merged into or acquired by hyperscalers or stronger players.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Neocloud failures likely transfer hard assets to hyperscalers rather than evaporate value.
insights.quote: this time around the neo clouds u have GPUs, they've got data centers

insights.claim: Because it is so hard to know which AI players will win or lose, Yardeni suggests investors might simply buy the Nasdaq 100 rather than pick individual AI stocks.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Index exposure is the preferred way to play AI given winner/loser uncertainty.
insights.quote: So maybe you just uh buy the NASDAQ 100 and call it a day.

insights.claim: Moratoriums, public opposition and expensive borrowing that slow data center construction would make existing operational data centers relatively scarce and raise the cost of compute, though builders will likely relocate to welcoming states and communities.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Barriers to new builds increase the value of existing data center capacity.

insights.claim: Yardeni says there is no real evidence that AI has led to major job losses on balance; employment has grown and the real issue is a shortage of workers.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: AI job-loss fears are not yet showing up in data.
insights.quote: What really have is a shortage of of workers.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 forward P/E has fallen back to about 18.2, roughly where it was on Liberation Day, while forward earnings are up about 49% since then, so the index is near record highs with a contracting multiple.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Market gains are earnings-driven, undermining the 1999-2000 bubble analogy.

insights.claim: Yardeni's 'FEMO beats FOMO' framework: fabulous earnings momentum is driving markets globally while fear of missing out fades, shown by falling P/Es alongside record forward earnings in the US and major world markets.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Multiples have room to re-rate if sentiment recovers since earnings are carrying the market.

insights.claim: An 18.2 forward P/E is attractive provided there is no recession and the economy keeps delivering earnings; Yardeni sees recession as very unlikely before the end of the decade.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: No-recession view implies limited further P/E downside.
insights.quote: I would argue that 18.2 is a pretty uh pretty attractive PE as long as you agree with me that there's not going to be recession

insights.claim: Using a crude Fed-model logic (1 divided by bond yield), a 5% 10-year yield is consistent with a forward P/E of about 20, and the relationship between bond yields and forward P/E appears to have tightened recently.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A 5% yield does not preclude a 20x multiple.
insights.quote: 5% is not inconsistent with a a 20 multiple.

insights.claim: Analysts typically start too optimistic and cut estimates, but they cut to still-bullish numbers; what they truly miss is recessions, so if no recession occurs, forward earnings estimates will be roughly right.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Estimate cuts are not bearish absent recession.

insights.claim: Analyst consensus has S&P 500 earnings rising about 16% in 2026 and another 16% in 2027, with the 2028 estimate at $494, nearly the $500 Yardeni had projected only for 2030.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Street estimates are more bullish than Yardeni's, suggesting upside risk to his targets.

insights.claim: Yardeni keeps his S&P 500 target of 10,000 by end-2029 (forward EPS $500 x 20 P/E) but acknowledges that if analysts' $500 for 2028 is right, the market could discount it and hit 10,000 by end-2027.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: 10,000 could arrive two years early.
insights.quote: Is it possible that we will get to 10,000 on the S&P 500 by the end of next year instead of by the end of 2029? Yeah, it's possible

insights.claim: Yardeni still expects a Santa Claus rally and an S&P 500 level of 7,900, and views Friday's AI selloff and the current dip as buying opportunities.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Year-end rally call intact; dips are to be bought.
insights.quote: we think there's still a Santa Claus rally coming and we're still looking for 7,900

insights.claim: Q3 S&P 500 earnings growth estimate dipped slightly to 23.8% after Google and Intel results, while Q4 is holding at about 30.2%, excluding any mark-to-market gains.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Earnings growth remains exceptionally strong into year-end.

insights.claim: Forward earnings for the S&P 500, S&P 400 midcaps and S&P 600 small caps are all at record highs, and the ex-Magnificent-7 ETF (XMAG) is up 14%, confirming broadening on the earnings side.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Broadening is fundamentally supported, not just a rotation.

insights.claim: Yardeni believes the Fed, which passed on a rate hike in October, held off for political reasons ahead of the midterms, and expects 25bp in December with an outside chance of 50bp, plus another 25bp early next year.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Rate-hike path is likely steeper than the market's reduced pricing.
insights.quote: I think there's an outside chance they'll do 50 basis points.

insights.claim: Cleveland Fed nowcasts show headline and core PCE inflation running with 3% handles year-over-year, well above the 2% target, while real GDP grew 3.4% and real final demand over 4%.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Strong growth plus sticky inflation justifies further hikes.

insights.claim: The recent calming of bond yields without any fix to fiscal deficits shows the yield rise was not a debt-crisis signal, and Yardeni says Ray Dalio has been too pessimistic on the debt issue for too long.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Debt-crisis narratives are overstated as a bond market driver.

insights.claim: Yardeni sees gold's fall from about $5,500 to below $4,000 as a correction, not the start of a bear market, and says gold still belongs in portfolios.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Gold dip is a correction within an ongoing uptrend.
insights.quote: Got up to 5,500 and now I don't think this is the beginning of a bare market. I still think this is a correction.

insights.claim: Gold has been weighed down by rising short-term rates, but central bank buying by countries the US doesn't get along with, such as China, Russia and Iran, is rate-insensitive and should lift prices; the bull case originated with the 2022 freezing of Russia's FX assets.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Geopolitically driven central bank demand underpins gold despite Fed hikes.

insights.claim: Yardeni Research moved from overweight to market weight on global equities, holding the US at about 65% of MSCI, while noting forward revenues and earnings for the All Country World ex-US are historically strong, partly due to South Korea and Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Neutral global allocation; non-US earnings strength is tech-hardware driven.

insights.claim: Yardeni continues to call China uninvestable, fine for trading only, citing the Invesco China Technology ETF (CQQQ) lagging the Nasdaq 100 (QQQ).
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Avoid long-term China equity exposure.

insights.claim: Polls show Republicans very likely to lose the House and possibly the Senate in the midterms; Yardeni expects partisanship to worsen but notes gridlock has often been viewed by the market as bullish.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Divided government is a market-friendly outcome.
insights.quote: Gridlock has very often uh been viewed by the market as a bullish development.
